forces.title: Concentrated Fuel Supply Chains for Next-Gen Reactors in Western Countries
forces.description: The nuclear fuel chain, particularly enrichment, is highly concentrated in a few global regions, and capacity for high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) required by next-generation reactors is limited in Western countries. This exposes European nuclear development to potential supply bottlenecks and geopolitical risks, hindering expansion plans for advanced reactor designs and increasing costs due to limited vendor competition and long lead times in securing essential materials for future nuclear projects.
forces.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

forces.title: Decline in Utility In-House Engineering Capabilities Impacts Project Execution
forces.description: Historically, French and other utilities maintained strong in-house engineering and project-delivery capabilities, which were crucial for successful nuclear construction programs. However, many European utilities have significantly reduced this internal capacity over time, leading to a loss of critical skills and increased reliance on external contractors and integrators. This structural shift contributes to increased project complexity, longer construction times, and greater risk of delays and cost overruns in new nuclear buildouts, including the current EPR2 program.
forces.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

forces.title: High Construction Costs and Capex Inefficiency in European Nuclear Projects
forces.description: Nuclear projects in France and other European countries face significantly higher total construction costs, adding $50-60 per megawatt-hour compared to efficient benchmarks like South Korea. This is driven by expensive direct costs, including labor and materials. Compounding this, capital expenditure inefficiency stems from longer construction times—up to two decades for recent projects—and bespoke designs, which keep capital at risk for extended periods, amplifying interest costs and project risks, thus increasing the overall levelized cost of energy in Europe.
forces.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

forces.title: Elevated Equipment and Financing Costs for French Nuclear Projects
forces.description: French nuclear projects incur higher equipment pricing, adding $14-20 per megawatt-hour to costs, due to the concentration of Tier 1 suppliers, limited global metal forging capacity, and bespoke specifications that restrict vendor competition. Furthermore, longer construction timelines, typical for complex projects like the European pressurized reactor 2 program, result in higher financing costs, adding roughly $15-20 per megawatt-hour. This is because capital remains at risk for extended periods, even with existing concessional financing from the French government.
forces.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

forces.title: Public Opposition and Fragmented Regulatory Oversight Impede Nuclear Development
forces.description: Concerns surrounding perceived nuclear safety and past decommissioning decisions, particularly evident in Germany, continue to impede the nuclear build-out in Europe. Furthermore, inconsistent policy support and fragmented regulatory oversight, as highlighted by a UK review noting up to eight regulators for a single project, create significant delays and cost increases. This regulatory uncertainty, coupled with varying public acceptance, presents a critical barrier to attracting investment and securing timely approvals for new nuclear energy projects across the EU.
forces.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

forces.title: Increased Government Financial and Policy Support for European Nuclear Programs
forces.description: European nuclear programs are increasingly benefiting from state-backed utilities and government-supported financing, including subsidized loans (e.g., France's EPR2 program) and loan guarantees. This robust policy landscape, reinforced by the EU Commission President acknowledging past anti-nuclear policy as a 'strategic mistake,' is designed to bolster developer confidence and significantly reduce financing costs. Such financial and policy tools are particularly crucial for high-risk first-of-a-kind projects, enabling them to proceed with greater certainty and attracting necessary private investment across Europe.
forces.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

forces.title: Weak Execution Track Record and Cost Overruns on European Nuclear Projects
forces.description: Nuclear projects globally, including those in Europe like Flamanville 3, have a weak delivery track record, with few completed on time and on budget. Flagship projects consistently face complexity, significant delays, and substantial cost overruns (e.g., Hinkley Point C in the UK, Flamanville). This history of execution challenges, often stemming from scope growth and governance bottlenecks, erodes investor confidence and highlights considerable hurdles for large-scale nuclear expansion in Europe, making new investments appear high-risk to capital allocators.
forces.source_title: Nuclear and Megaproject Delivery: Five Elements That Predict Success

forces.title: Immature Nuclear-Qualified Supply Chain and Workforce in Western Countries
forces.description: Decades without new nuclear builds in Western countries have led to the atrophy of the nuclear-qualified workforce, component suppliers, and heavy construction base. This immaturity means supply chains currently lack the necessary scale and expertise to support a rapid nuclear expansion. Rebuilding this crucial industrial ecosystem requires significant, long-term investment in multi-year apprenticeships and vendor qualification programs, posing a structural challenge that contributes to delays and increased costs for new projects in Europe.
forces.source_title: Making the Nuclear Final Investment Decision the Right Way

forces.title: Operational Disruptions and Climate Vulnerability Impact French Nuclear Output
forces.description: French nuclear output can be significantly impacted by operational disruptions, including outages for extensive repair work and severe droughts affecting cooling water availability for power plants. During the 2022 energy crisis, over 50% of France's nuclear fleet was out of operation due to repair, highlighting a vulnerability to both maintenance issues and climate-related events. These disruptions lead to reduced generation, necessitating increased imports and impacting overall energy security and reliability for France and neighboring European countries.
forces.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

forces.title: European Countries Reconsidering and Lifting Nuclear Bans
forces.description: Several European countries, including Spain, Italy, Belgium, Denmark, and Lithuania, are actively reconsidering or reversing previous nuclear bans. This significant policy shift reflects a growing commitment to nuclear power's role in Europe's future energy landscape, driven by heightened energy security imperatives and ambitious decarbonization goals. This re-evaluation of national energy strategies unlocks new markets and substantial investment opportunities for nuclear energy development across the continent, potentially leading to increased capacity and a more resilient energy mix.
forces.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

forces.title: SMR Deployment Immaturity and Dependence on Russian Advanced Nuclear Fuel
forces.description: While Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) are generating significant interest for their potential benefits in standardization and modular construction, their deployment in Europe is still in very early stages. Globally, only a few SMRs are operational, and widespread commercialization is years away. Furthermore, these advanced reactors often rely on specialized nuclear fuel that is primarily sourced from Russia. This dependence introduces significant geopolitical risks and potential supply vulnerabilities for Europe, complicating SMR adoption and limiting their immediate impact on energy security.
forces.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

forces.title: Resumption and Expansion of French Nuclear Capacity Bolsters European Supply
forces.description: The French nuclear fleet, a cornerstone of European power generation, has seen a significant resumption of operations in 2024 following extensive repair work, leading to an upward revision of EDF's production forecasts (335-365 TWh for 2025). This recovery, coupled with EDF's strong capital expenditure commitments for new nuclear plants and French government measures like the MATCH program for workforce development, enhances domestic supply. This allows for increased electricity exports to neighboring countries, significantly improving regional energy stability and grid resilience across Europe.
forces.source_title: European Utilities: A bittersweet year for earnings

viewpoints.title: Nuclear Power Renaissance Driven by Demand, Decarbonization, and Security
viewpoints.description: McKinsey states that nuclear power is experiencing a renaissance due to the surging demand for electricity from AI data centers and electrification, coupled with global efforts to reduce carbon emissions. Additionally, an increased focus on energy security and geopolitical resilience has heightened interest. The firm cites IAEA projections that global nuclear power generation could more than double by 2050, driven by new plant installations and emerging Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) which offer benefits in standardization and manufacturing efficiency.
viewpoints.source_title: Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making

viewpoints.title: France's Nuclear Generation Shields Electricity Prices from Gas Shocks
viewpoints.description: BCG Global highlights that France's significant nuclear generation capacity plays a crucial role in insulating its electricity prices from wholesale gas price shocks, unlike other European countries. By relying less on gas for electricity generation, France maintains a lower electricity-to-gas price ratio, contributing to greater energy security and price stability. This model demonstrates the strategic advantage of a diversified energy mix with a strong nuclear component in mitigating market volatility.
viewpoints.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

viewpoints.title: Nuclear Investment Rising, But Delivery Challenges Persist Globally
viewpoints.description: Bain & Company acknowledges a rising interest in nuclear investment globally, driven by increased electricity demand and decarbonization goals. However, the firm cautions that nuclear projects face persistent delivery challenges, with few completed on time and on budget. This suggests that while the strategic case for nuclear power is strengthening, the industry must overcome historical issues related to execution, project management, and construction efficiency to fully capitalize on this renewed interest.
viewpoints.source_title: Nuclear and Megaproject Delivery: Five Elements That Predict Success

viewpoints.title: EU President Calls Europe's Past Nuclear Phase-Out a 'Strategic Mistake'
viewpoints.description: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen publicly stated in March 2026 that Europe's decision to shift away from nuclear energy following the Fukushima disaster, particularly Germany's abrupt phase-out, was a 'strategic mistake.' This high-level acknowledgment signals a significant policy shift within the EU, supporting a renewed commitment to nuclear power as a vital component for energy security and decarbonization efforts, potentially paving the way for further investment and project development.
viewpoints.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

viewpoints.title: Nuclear Energy: Key Long-Term Solution for Europe's Energy Independence
viewpoints.description: ING Think views a comprehensive electrification strategy, powered by renewables and nuclear energy, as the most effective long-term solution for Europe. This approach is critical to break the link between electricity costs and volatile global gas prices, thereby enhancing energy independence and stability. The 2022 energy crisis reignited interest in nuclear power, paralleling France's historical large-scale buildout, which significantly contributes to its reliable and low-cost electricity supply today.
viewpoints.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

viewpoints.title: Europe's Nuclear Capacity Expansion Faces Long-Term Challenges Despite Interest
viewpoints.description: ING Think highlights that while Europe has renewed interest in nuclear power, significantly expanding its capacity will be a challenging and uncertain long-term endeavor, likely taking many years. Key hurdles include the demonstrated complexity, costliness, and delays of recent large-scale nuclear projects (e.g., Flamanville), alongside the early stage of Small Modular Reactor (SMR) deployment. Furthermore, geopolitical risks associated with relying on Russian-sourced advanced nuclear fuel for SMRs complicate adoption and increase supply vulnerability.
viewpoints.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

viewpoints.title: Extending Existing Nuclear Plant Lifecycles is a 'No Regret Policy'
viewpoints.description: ING Think considers extending the lifecycle of existing and low-cost nuclear power plants in Europe to be a 'no regret policy.' This approach offers a practical and immediate way to secure reliable, low-carbon electricity generation without the significant capital and time investments associated with new builds. This viewpoint underscores the value of maintaining and optimizing current nuclear assets as part of Europe's energy strategy, especially in light of ongoing energy security concerns and decarbonization goals.
viewpoints.source_title: How Europe can reduce reliance on imported gas and what it means for business…

Global efforts to reduce carbon emissions require expansion of low-emissions power generation sources like nuclear power.
Additional focus on geopolitical resilience and securing stable energy supply, especially after disruptions, drives interest in domestic, reliable sources.

Imperatives for stable grid operations and meeting carbon reduction commitments drive investment into firm clean power sources like nuclear.
